utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence had one preliminary matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yesterday Your Honours had asked for assistance to locate the particular Article 60 of the Geneva Conventions that was the subject of the discussion as to the -- self-defence upon being attacked. We have two witnesses who have provided evidence as to that. The first is GRM097 at transcript page 40083 -- pardon me, 40085, line 13, through 40086, line 25. And the second is the witness we have today, the expert, Mr. Kovac, in his expert report, 1D5358, page 189, paragraph 5.2 of the same, where it is described as Article 60 of Chapter V under the heading: "Localities and zones under special protection" of the protocol additional to the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949. And Mr. Kovac specifically references paragraph 7 of Article 6 [sic] of this protocol. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is not about self-defence primarily but not indeed as the self-defence as understood in Article 51 of the UN Charter. That's a different kind of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I better understand now what you were referring to. That's ... Yes. Thank you for that information, Mr. Ivetic. I'd like to briefly move into private session before we re-start with Witness Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back in court, Mr. Kovac. It takes a while to get in and out. We regret that, but we were unable to change it. We'd rather would have preferred to hear your evidence in one flow, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we hope to conclude today. Perhaps needless to remind you, but I still have to do, to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. McCloskey will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you know, we're continuing the Prosecution cross-examination as the -- as Mr. President told you, and you haven't had a chance to answer my questions as yet. But hopefully if you listen to the question and answer briefly, we'll be able to all leave in a short time. Mr. Ivetic spoke to you in direct examination and you answered questions briefly about the time-period that General Mladic was outside the RS and the rules related to whether a person would take over command or not. Let me read you the question that Mr. Ivetic gave you and your answer, and then I'll ask you a couple of questions on this point. And this was at page 41393 of the transcript, and the question by Mr. Ivetic was: "And by operation of the rules, of regulations, who would be that someone on the ground who commands when the commander is away?" And your answer: "In this specific case, there was no obligation for the commander of the Main Staff to be present constantly. His second-in-command is the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic in this instant case, who was dealing with problems in the western part of the theatre of war, in Krajina, in the area of operation of the 1st and 2nd Corps, because there was already intelligence that the Croatian army and the BiH army were planning an incursion into the area of the VRS. Documents were signed by General Gvero when Mladic was absent. According to the rules, it was possible for a member of the command, the eldest officer in a certain area, to represent the Main Staff, and I believe in this case that's what happened." Now, from your study of the materials, what dates after the fall of Srebrenica was Mladic absent from the RS?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the documents that I analysed, it was 14 to 17 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware of the agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence that General Mladic crossed over into Serbia the afternoon of 14 July from the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly about which crossing it was because it wasn't relevant to me, but it was the period that was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mention in your testimony that documents were signed by General Gvero when Mladic was absent. What documents were signed by General Gvero on the 14th, 15th, and 16th of July? You don't have any in your report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned two documents. One of the documents, I think, is referenced in the report, and it relates to the treatment of prisoners and the need for increased security measures in the zone through which the column from Srebrenica was trying to break through and search of the terrain. That document was of 13 July, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, it was the 13th of July. But that was not the period that General Mladic was out of the RS, was it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But he must have been outside of that zone because I don't see otherwise why General Gvero would have signed this document on the 13th. I think already on the 13th, Gvero was the most senior officer from the Main Staff in the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you learn from your study of the documents that not only was General Milovanovic in the Krajina, but General Tolimir was in Zepa and General Gvero was at the Main Staff headquarters in Han Pijesak on the 13th of July? You agree?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you learn from studies of your materials that on the 13th of July that General Mladic was with his troops on the ground in and around the Bratunac area, the Sandici meadow area, the Nova Kasaba area, and on the evening of the 13th of July in the Vlasenica command post?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on the 13th of July at the Vlasenica command post, General Mladic held a small ceremony and -- where he announced that General Krstic was now the commander of the Drina Corps and General Zivanovic was not. Did you learn that as well?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now this question of the ceremony, it was the usual way of imparting information during military operations to say that somebody else took over the duties of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And did you -- were you able to watch the testimony or read the testimony of Richard Butler, one of the Prosecution military experts, in this case?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you read the part of the testimony where he went over documents in Mladic's name and orders from General Mladic on the 14th and 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to another topic. I want to ask you about some parts of your report, which we'll recall is 65 ter 1D5358, which I hope to be able to refer to as "the report" after that. And if we could go to page 238 in the English and page 235 in the B/C/S, and I want to draw your attention to some parts that are in your paragraph 5.162. You'll see it come up on the board. And you'll note that right after your underlined part at 5.162, you say: "After the commission of the crimes against captured members of the 28th ABH Division, the Muslim leadership ..." and you go on. Well, I now want to skip a few lines but you can go ahead and read those to yourself, the following lines, as we go down, and start with about the last third of the paragraph. And I think you're going to -- we're going to have to go to page 236 in the B/C/S so you can read along. You note, and I believe you're referring to the crime against captured members of the 28th Division as you begin this: "This crime had not been planned by the political and military leadership of Republika Srpska. It was probably designed in order for the media to prepare the international community and public to accept the consequences of the operations executed by the Croatian army, the ARBH and the HVO, with NATO air, intelligence and logistics support, in which ethnic cleansing and crimes in the area of Republic of Serbian Krajina in Croatia were committed as well as in the western part of Republika Srpska in BH, when about 2300 soldiers and civilians were killed and over 220.000 people expelled from their homes. The international public neither saw or heard of these crimes, for the crime in Srebrenica was a screen for continuing the genocide against the Serbian people in Croatia and BH which started in the Ustasha NDH and continued in the final operations in the civil war in 1995." Now, you say in this thesis, manifesto maybe, that the crimes, "it was probably designed in order for the media to prepare ..." Tell us, what has your investigations --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the question to be completed, but if counsel said he is going to refer to it as "the report" and now he's referred to it as "the thesis" and "the manifesto," we're -- instead of making things more simplified, we're making it more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is -- Mr. McCloskey was quoting the report and added some comment which is perhaps not needed, but let's wait for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's view that this is a thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. It wasn't a question. Of course, unless you want to ask now whether this is a thesis or not, and, of course, such a discussion will end in nothing. It is to some extent argument. Apart from that, it's all probability the expert describes. But you'd like to know what the basis is for this assessment of the probability, because that seemed to be your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm getting into all these -- I'm trying to get into all these but I can make it simpler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, in your study of these materials, can you tell us who do you think it was or what was it that was the designer of this thing that you described? You say "it was probably designed in order for the media," you're referring to the crimes in Srebrenica. Who do you think designed this, if it wasn't the Republika Srpska leaders or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to note that there can be no mention of any thesis or manifest or a subjective view. The numbers given in this very paragraph are historical facts, and that's why I did not further explain them. As for the specific answer to your question, while studying the activities of various actors or factors that exerted influence on the occurrence of the crime in Srebrenica, I recognised three distinct players. One is part of the international community; second, the leadership of the Muslims in Sarajevo, both political and military; and, three, the military and political leadership of Serbia. All these players had a direct impact on the positions that I expressed relative to the operation in Srebrenica. I believe that this crime towards the end of the war was the least necessary to the military and political leadership of the Serbs. Unfortunately, following some decisions after the entry into Srebrenica, this crime unfortunately occurred. I will remind you of the discussions of General Morillon at that time with the Serbian President Milosevic, when he said that it shouldn't be allowed for Serbs to enter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Excuse me, sir, we know that there were international and other forces involved. What you say here is that it's -- the crime was not designed by RS and the VRS. You say it was probably designed in order to do something or other. Who do you think probably designed it if it's not the Serbs, it's not the Serb army or the Serb civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a great part of the impact on the events in Srebrenica towards -- through the Muslim and Serb leaderships was exerted by part of the structures of the international community, and that the decisions both in Sarajevo as well as the decisions of Bosnian Serbs were unreasonable and irrational. Among the Serbian political leadership --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, sir, it was a simple question. I'll go on to another question. Let's stay on your report. Let's go to page 184 in the English and page 182 in the B/C/S. And let's look at paragraph 5.4. Why don't you read that a bit to yourself for a minute. But what I want to read out and ask you about are the last about six lines of this paragraph. And that section is -- is this: "When all these major issues are reviewed, it is possible to speak more objectively about whether command responsibility attaches to General ... Mladic for the crimes that happened, or whether those crimes happened according to someone else's plan, drawing on ethnic hatred and the vast revenge potential and using mercenaries at the recommendation of those who steered the war in BH and who needed the tragedy in Srebrenica to ethnically cleanse and expel Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and from the western part of Republika Srpska." So here again, sir, you pose in a question whether these crimes happened according to someone else's plan. Who -- whose plan? Who's the "someone else" besides the -- General Mladic, the VRS, or the RS authorities?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several places in my report, it is indicated - and I just started to say that a moment ago when I was interrupted - as to who else was involved in this. Over the past few years, we've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir --

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- several testimonies by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not my question. That's not my question. We've heard a lot about people being involved in this. Whose plan was it, if you know? You referred to someone else's plan not the RS. Who else planned it, if you know? If you don't know, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know. I know. But I am not allowed to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can tell us who -- who planned and you can explain your answer but you need to answer the question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this manner of badgering the witness by Mr. McCloskey. If you look at the answer that was started to given by the witness, he's talking about who's involved in the planning, and Mr. McCloskey interrupts him and says: Answer my question. He is twice now tried to answer the question and has been interrupted. If Mr. McCloskey does not want this evidence, that shouldn't be -- he shouldn't be allowed to badger the witness as if he is not answering the question when he is trying to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when you said that the witness said -- started his answer by saying who was involved in the planning, he said who was involved which is not necessarily at the planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I beg to differ. He says "involved in this." If the question is related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- planning and it says "involved in this," it's planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're interrupting me which you're supposed not to do. It was just the first sentence of what I wanted to say. Witness, if you would first tell us who it was or who they were to whom you referred as someone else's plan, and then explain - and that may even be the follow-up question - why you think that it was them that planned rather than, as you said, someone who is charged? Could you please tell us who it is, or who they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the report I presented the findings that pertained to these people. Primarily on the basis of the statements of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You say on whose authority. Who are you referring to? You said: "I presented the findings that pertain to these people." Please tell us who "these people" are. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically it is a quotation, an interview of a journalist with Alija Izetbegovic, and he mentions that he spoke to Clinton --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you -- stop you there. Do you want to say that it is Mr. Izetbegovic who was the one or one of those who planned it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the participants -- no, not planned the crime, no. No. Let's be clear. Planned the departure from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think we were talking about the crimes, but -- so it was Mr. Izetbegovic. Any other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And his conversation with Clinton. And also presenting the results of his conversation and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not -- I'm not asking about conversations. I'm asking who that other person is. Do I understand you that you deduced from that conversation that Mr. Clinton was one of the other planners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not of the crime. The operation, yes, the operation in the sense of departing from the area of Srebrenica and the safe area. One of the witnesses in that respect is the chief of the SUP or MUP in the municipality of Srebrenica, Mr. Meholjic, and I present his reports and I reviewed a great deal of material where he precisely says what President Izetbegovic told him as far back as 1993 in Sarajevo. And the agreement to exchange -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- you're now moving away from the question because what was read to you was about responsibility for the crimes. That was the portion that was read to you from page 182 of your report, and you're now moving away from it and saying, well, others were responsible for -- for what may have happened or withdrawal or whatever. But you're talking about crimes in page 182, and I think that Mr. McCloskey is focusing on who you consider to be responsible for the planning of those crimes. Now, you've mentioned two names: Izetbegovic, Clinton. And you've also said that those you consider not to be responsible for the crimes but for whatever they did in relation to Srebrenica. Do you have names of those you consider to be responsible for the planning of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything I said previously does not pertain to the planning of crimes. Or participation. I mean, I'm directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. Okay, fine. The question was focusing on where you wrote: "... or whether those crimes happened according to someone else's plan," that is, someone else having a plan that those crimes will be committed. But I do now understand that the persons you mentioned, that you don't consider them to be responsible for the planning of the crimes, the planning which resulted in the crimes. My question is: Do you have any other names? If so, please tell them; if not, I'll invite Mr. McCloskey to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that at this top level nobody planned crimes directly, a strategic level, neither in Republika Srpska or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that wasn't the question, as a matter of fact. But, Mr. McCloskey, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this part of read out to you, it's not footnoted. You noted earlier with Mr. Weber that much of your material came from General Radinovic. Are you getting the ideas expressed or the statements expressed in what I read out from Radinovic or is -- from General Radinovic, or is this a result of your own thought?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the entire material analysed, these are the results or conclusions of my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that include General Radinovic's work for this particular part?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this particular position, I did not see any conclusions of his to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go now to 1D06016, page 66 in the English, page 68 in the B/C/S, and this is a report that General Radinovic made for the Krstic Defence in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to remind us of what we previously saw in your report you said: "... drawing on ethnic hatred and the vast revenge potential and using mercenaries at the recommendation of those who steered the war in the BH." So I want to ask you about mercenaries a bit. Because we see here in the -- in this paragraph and I'll start reading where it says "Goran Matic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is where, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the fifth line down in the English and it is B/C/S page 68. It's 4.3 paragraph. And we see it really -- yeah, right there. They've found it - thank you - in the middle of the page, the cursor found it. But, of course, the witness can take a little extra time to read the whole 4.3 so he can put it in context. If -- though I'm not really sure it needs to be, from my perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So here General Radinovic says: "Goran Matic, the federal Republic of Yugoslavia information minister, talked about the massacre of Muslim civilians at a press conference when giving information about results of the investigation conducted against ... Pauk (Spider) group. That group consisted of paid Croats, Slovenes, Muslims, and Serbs." Now General Radinovic goes on to say: "French intelligence service organised, equipped, and trained the group to perform the massacre on [sic] Muslim civilians with the aim of attributing that crime to the Serbs and declaring the Serb military and political strategy to be criminal and the Republika Srpska as a political result of a world crime. After that scenario, all violence against the Serbs became legitimate." Now simple question. In your previous paragraph, you refer to mercenaries. Are these the mercenaries that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only they. Skorpions, mercenaries, the crime they committed against prisoners in Srebrenica, a regular, normal Serb soldier would never do anything like that; that is to say, shooting prisoners in the back and recording that. That is preparing and documenting crimes and that can only be done by mercenaries for a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you find these -- this statement of General Radinovic credible that I just read out?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that group only. I've just mentioned the Skorpions, primarily. In my view, this is a paramilitary group that was not under military control. I actually spoke about the example of a crime that could be committed only by mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you do find this credible but you want to add to it people like the Skorpions and others?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about principled conduct. An individual paramilitary organisation or mercenaries, I cannot speak about that in detail. But I have mentioned an example of something that I studied to a greater extent. That's the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simple question: Is Radinovic's statement credible?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe there's a problem with interpretation. In what sense do you mean "credible".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can go on. Let's go to your report at page 232 in the English, page 230 in the B/C/S. It's paragraph 5.143. And you do in your report talk repeatedly about people that you believe are responsible for the killings on the ground, and the part I would read to you is: "The mass crimes of executing the prisoners were probably committed by self-organised paramilitary groups from Podrinje, coming from pre-war criminal milieus, as well as by groups of 'avengers,' whose family members had been killed during the war by members of the 28th ABH Division. They probably committed these crimes in co-operation with some officers from security structures or even on the recommendation and under the influence of external factors which had an impact on the course of the development of the war [sic] in the BH." Okay. These avengers that were -- and these self-organised paramilitaries, what has your investigation revealed? What sort -- who did they have co-operation with? You say you think they had co-operations with some officers from the security structures. Which officers from the security structures did these groups that self-organised?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw in the documents is the link between what happened on the ground and the members of the security service, part of the units of the military police, and parts of -- or, rather, units from the Drina Corps. But the co-ordination of all those developments went through this security structure and the distribution of prisoners in the area of the Zvornik Brigade. So I'm referring specifically to the officers of the security organ, starting with the security organ of the Drina Corps to the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade, as the persons that are most frequently mentioned in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the security organ of the Main Staff? Did you find that in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Yes, mentioned in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was it fair to say you believe that the security organ of the Main Staff, the security organ of the Drina Corps, and the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade co-operated on the ground with those that summarily executed the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense, co-operated. But that they were involved in this entire endeavour of transferring prisoners, yes. Primarily the organs of security of the corps and the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying that you don't know in what sense to co-operate. Is it not in the sense of co-operation as you have used the word in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in co-operation with an exchange of information concerning prisoners, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you don't define it in the paragraph. You just say "co-operation." And I suppose that's how the question is also phrased. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, tell us. Who are the security officers of the Main Staff that were involved in this co-operation with the people involved in the killings?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Beara, I think, from the level of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From the Glavni Stab, the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Main Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the Drina Corps security organ person that was involved with the same co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel ... right now I simply cannot remember his last name. But I remember his rank. It was that of a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you for your assistance. Yes. Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Zvornik Brigade security officer, Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Vujadin Popovic's superior officer and commander was General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Colonel Beara's immediate superior was General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Colonel Beara's commander was Commander Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was his commander, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly. There was not a direct chain of command involved. It was through General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And these security organs played a significant role in the murders, would you say?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how big was the role played by each and every one of them, I cannot say. I cannot say that it was the chief of security of the Drina Corps or the Zvornik Brigade is responsible for the crime committed against prisoners in such a place or such a place, but they are the ones that most often appear in documents. That is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I think you know, but we're not asking you to give us a numerical count of how often people appear in documents. We're getting your opinion that these security officers were involved in the conduct of the crimes that were carried out. They helped co-ordinate with the people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes, but they are the ones that were responsible in terms of competence; that is to say, how prisoners of war should be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to your -- another part of your report. It's page 228 in the English and 226 in the B/C/S. It's under 5.134. And I want to start -- it's about seven lines up from the bottom of 5.134, but take a look at the whole 5.134 so you can get a feel for it. And on this -- I think on the subject matter we've been talking about you say: "It is obvious that the decision to transport the prisoners from Bratunac to the area of the Zvornik Brigade could not have involved anyone from the Zvornik Brigade command. Only the security organs of the superior commands of the Drina Corps and the VRS Main Staff could have decided that." So when -- as the Court had seen in this case that when busloads of Muslims were transported on the evening of 13 July from Bratunac to the school at Orahovac near Zvornik, and many, many hundreds, in fact, thousands were transported from Bratunac to schools around Zvornik area on the 14th of July, you're concluding here that only the -- Beara and Popovic could have decided that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found only that communication in documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you think they're the ones that played a role in that -- in that movement of prisoners, Beara and Popovic? Or do you -- are you just telling us what's in -- what documents show again?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they made the decision for the transfer of prisoners, and it was an unreasonable decision. And the commander of the Zvornik Brigade says that in his interim report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that Colonel Ljubisa Beara is acting unknown to General Mladic and not under General Mladic's orders? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that is the case. Because these are questions that have to do with putting up prisoners and, unfortunately, it was done the wrong way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have one question in relation to this point. If it was not under the direction of General Mladic, are you aware of any disciplinary measures that Mr. Mladic may have taken against these two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that, but that was after finding out, after getting information about the crime, when it was still fresh, probably in August, when other events put distance between that period and Srebrenica. And, of course, I know that he has disciplinary jurisdiction. He could have taken disciplinary measures. But these offences are criminal offences, and that's not something that belongs under command responsibility and the chain of command. Except to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll follow up after break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we take that break, I think the parties have received some work product of this witness. I think we had asked you to bring military documents you -- you referred to that and you said you had available. Now, what was delivered through the intermediary of the Victims and Witness Section, I couldn't read it, I haven't even tried to read it, but at first glance, it didn't look that much as a military document. I decided that it would be made available to the parties so that they could do with it whatever they wished to do with it. There is a copy without a translation in the hands of Chamber's staff and we're not -- at this moment I think we don't have anyone who can read the language. So we just have it there and wait and see what the parties will do with it. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's understood, your communication. With respect to the document, though, the Prosecution doesn't view it as responsive to just the information and list that was requested. In our brief review of it and attempted review with the translation, it appears to be a further analysis now citing some things. So that was just would be our position right now. We don't have a full translation available to obviously appropriately appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any further comments on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours the footnote number 1 is a book by a BiH military commander that he is citing to and I believe that the figures come from the book. I have not had a chance to locate the book to check, but it would appear that the witness is attempting to show where some of this information comes from. But it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- may not be all-inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he said he had military documents or a military document available which he could provide and it -- I do understand from you now that there is a footnote that may refer to any document but what was provided is not a military document or military documents in itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's a reference to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think, Witness, that's what you said you had available, a military document or military documents, and we just established at this moment that the parties consider what you provided is not a military document or military documents you referred to. I leave to that at this moment. We'll take a break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to briefly deal with the testimony anticipated of Mr. Stankovic on, if I could say so, Dunjic evidence. The Chamber would like to have it very clear now what -- where we are and put that on the record. Where we are is what apparently the parties have -- an approach the parties have agreed upon in relation to Mr. Stankovic's role with regard to the Dunjic expert report. We do understand that the Dunjic expert report will not and is not tendered pursuant to Rule 94 bis (C). Instead, Mr. Stankovic will annotate the Dunjic report. The thus annotated Dunjic report will then be tendered as Mr. Stankovic's expert report. As Mr. Stankovic has not yet been recognised as an expert by the Chamber, the Chamber expects the Defence to follow the procedure of Rule 94 bis, including filing the annotated report, and the Chamber instructs the Defence to include updates on Mr. Stankovic's progress in relation to the Dunjic report in its weekly updates. Has this Chamber well understood what approach the parties agreed upon? And meanwhile, I think the witness can be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, and I -- that does reflect what the Prosecution would like to agree on. Because of the busyness of everyone that's what we were talking, but I do think we need to hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I could safely say that is what we will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's agreed. That's hereby then clarified. And we'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, we'll continue. I think it would save time if you more directly respond to questions put to you by Mr. McCloskey, rather than to first deal with a few other matters which are not part of the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Staying in your report, 65 ter 1D5358, let's go to page 208 in the English and 206 in the B/C/S. I'd like to look at paragraph 5.83 and 5.84. This is where you talk about Directive 7 and Directive 7.1, and I'll read this out briefly. "It is not disputed that Directive 7 bears the signature of Dr. Karadzic, just as it is not disputed that General Radivoje Miletic signed it as the person who was involved in its drafting. It is also beyond dispute that the cover letter with which the directive was distributed to the corps commands was signed by ... chief of the VRS GS, General Manojlo Milovanovic." Paragraph 5.84: "The RS president signed documents proposed to him by the VRS GS with confidence. A directive is not an executive document, but a whole series of executive documents is prepared on its basis in the form of commands, orders, plans and similar which offered possibilities for correcting what was not formulated well in the directive. Some ten days after it was issued, General Staff directive number 7/1 was drawn up. Its number indicates that it is a follow-up document to Directive 7. It is important to note that Directive 7/1 altered a few elements contained in Directive 7, primarily by omitting the incriminatory sentence on the tasks of the Drina Corps. That means that there was no intention to put civilians in jeopardy and that this formulation can be attributed to the poor judgement of an operations officer from the VRS GS who wrote the document and that this mistake was later noticed and removed from the new combat document, VRS GS Directive number 7.1." Now to discuss this briefly, let's go to Directive 7 itself which begins at P01469, page 1. And, General, we should see the cover page that you referred to in your report that went out by -- from -- under General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, it should be page 1 of 1469. There we go. Thank you. In the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, that's what you were referring to in your report, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll try to remember that this is dated 17 March 1995 when the directive is sent out to the corps. Let's go to page 2. And, General, is it your understanding this is the first page of the actual Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's page 3 in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for our memory, we'll note that that is dated March 8th. And I think we can all agree that this was at the last page signed by President Karadzic with a note drafted Colonel Radivoje Miletic, perhaps, and save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we could go to the body of the document. Yes, all right. Thank you for pulling that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what you also said in your report, that it was -- I think you said signed by, but we can see here that it's just typed, that it was drafted by Radivoje Miletic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the typewritten name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to the Drina Corps section, which should be page 17 in both languages, I believe. I'm sorry, it's page 10 in the English, 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to remind us, what you had said in your report is you talk about that 7.1 omitted what you call the "incriminatory sentence." So can we agree that the incriminatory sentence you referred to is -- is at the bottom of the page in English and is the -- near the end of the first paragraph in the Serbian and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First paragraph of the reference to Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe you meant by the incriminatory sentence: "By well-planned and well-thought out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Is that what you meant when you said that, that that was the incriminatory sentence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I meant that sentence, which is not in keeping with the logic of the directive or its intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question by saying that that was the sentence you referred to. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to your report at page 206 in the B/C/S and page 209, you say that that sentence, and I quote, "can be attributed to the poor judgement of an operations officer from the VRS GS who wrote the document, and that this mistake," you call it, "that this mistake was later noticed and removed from the new combat document." So who, in your view, is this operations officer who can be blamed for this statement?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know by name, but I believe it was very poor judgement and very badly formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know that General Miletic was the chief of operations and training in the Main Staff. So you're not referring to him as the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is certainly headed the drafting of the directive, but he was not the only one who participated in its drafting. He had an operative officer next to him and people who actually did the writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're saying that it's not Miletic that made this mistake. It was one of his staff, perhaps a lieutenant or a major?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, and officers of such ranks are not with the staff organ. They would have to be more senior officers, both by rank and by age. But it's not up to the chief of the operative organ to be -- in fact, he is responsible. He bears responsibility for this formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You go on to say here that it was a mistake and it was later noticed and removed. So are you telling us that you believe that this document that went out, that was signed by Karadzic on the 8th and it went out a few days later, was missed, this mistake was missed by Miletic, it was missed by President Karadzic, it was missed by General Mladic and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was noticed - that was my logic - it was removed in the following directive. But the document had gone out already. That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, Directive 7/1 - which we don't need go to - P1470, was -- went out on 31 March 1995. So your analysis takes this, not even to an officer, perhaps to a sergeant or a corporal that wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't understand each other. I said the person responsible is the one who signs the document, and in this specific case, that was Colonel - later General - Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in your report, when you refer to an operations officer, you meant Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He bears essential responsibility. But I mentioned in my report that this was imprudently done by an operations officer who phrased these items in the directive. However, it was Miletic's duty to review and revise the whole text and approve it before giving it to the supreme commander to sign. That's why I'm saying he is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we understand that, General. My point is: Are you saying that it was Miletic that phrased this or one of his subordinate officers, because you don't say it in your statement. You say: "It can" -- and I quote, "can be contributed to the poor judgement of an operations from the VRS GS." So the phraseology was not done by Miletic but someone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago that he didn't physically write it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please try to answer -- please try to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll object, Your Honours. He's answered the question twice. Counsel is refusing to listen to the answer. I'll give you the citations in a moment. In --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can go on without this tirade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, if the question is being posed, if the witness is being told he's not answering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I have a right to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- for the record show that is he wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you first not continue talking when I try to resolve a matter. If there's an objection, Mr. McCloskey, we'll first listen to that, and if you then later decide to go on and not put the question to the witness, that's fine. But the Defence has an opportunity to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Line -- page 28, line 17, the witness explicitly stated he did not know the name of the officer who drafted it. When he was asked by Mr. McCloskey whether it was a lieutenant or major, page 29, lines 2 through 6, the witness said it couldn't be a lieutenant or major because the officer would have to be of a more senior rank and a more seniority position. So he -- the witness has answered twice the question that Prosecution counsel is accusing him of not answering and that is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I think, first, if I look at the two spots you said, the first time he said he didn't know who it was. The second was that he didn't know rank. And now the question was: But was it somebody else than Mr. Miletic. That could be -- have been implied in his answers but I think that's what Mr. McCloskey would like to have clear. But since he said he would move on anyhow, I think that ... I think that there's certainly some merit in your objection, although literally you can't say that the same question was answered already. But before we move on, I have one other question for the witness where he apparently, at least in my view, Mr. Ivetic, didn't fully answer the question, which was -- you were asked whether when Directive 7 was issued, whether Karadzic and Mladic and - who else was it? - had missed that mistake. You didn't directly answer that question. You said when it was later noticed, the text was changed. But do I understand that implicit in this answer is that in the first round, before the mistake was noticed, as you said, that they missed the mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said twice that Miletic was responsible because he signed the document before it was sent out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard that. But the question was whether Miletic, Karadzic, and Mladic would have missed that mistake. Is that implicit in the answers you did give, that they have missed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all these persons were involved in this process that you mentioned in your question. The chief of operations forwards it to the supreme commander for signature. That's why I believe he is responsible, regardless of who put this language in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Did Miletic miss it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Karadzic miss it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in that position, a person doesn't ever have time enough to read the details of the document, he just signs. He missed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mladic miss it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he had any contact with this directive at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- that's -- now we have an answer to the question. If you are referring to later noticing the mistake, you relied on your logic of the matters. Is there anything else apart from your logic which makes you believe that it was a mistake which was then noticed and was then corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's an answer to my question. It's your logic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we saw that Milovanovic sent copies of this out. Did he miss it, the language, General Milovanovic, from your logic or knowledge of facts?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic only forwarded the directive. He wasn't responsible in that process to read the document before signing either, and maybe he noticed it after the document was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does your logic tell you that then-Colonel Miletic sent this document directly to President Karadzic without Mladic or Milovanovic seeing it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they saw some elements, or maybe they were familiar with elements of the directive, but they didn't have to read it in detail carefully. I'm talking about their job description, their competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to a document. Perhaps that may shed some light on the intentions of those that wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1505.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a document that's in evidence here, it's dated 4th of July. You will have a chance to see it. It's from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade at the time, Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. And he said some things in this document that, from the Prosecution's perspective, are remarkable similar to what you call the incriminatory sentence and so I want to ask you about this. And if you see, we have the first page there from Ognjenovic's document. It starts off with: "During his recent visit to our corps command, the commander of the VRS GS indicated that he would soon visit some of the corps units, including the Bratunac Brigade." Okay. Then Ognjenovic continue -- says to his -- to this particular unit, the 3rd Infantry Battalion, several things. And we can tell from this first page that Blagojevic was aware that Mladic had made some comments. So I want to go to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you said Blagojevic. Was that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. As we know, Blagojevic became commander of the Bratunac Brigade in May of 1995, and Ognjenovic was commander of the Bratunac Brigade in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You wanted to say Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I should have said Ognjenovic. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's look at -- it's under paragraph -- should be noted as -- well, it's right above what is noted as number 3 in both languages, and it starts, the part that I'm interested in: "We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task - the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Now what I'm particularly interested in are not the references to the enemy and defeating the enemy and driving the enemy out. What I'm asking about is, isn't this targeting this civilian population when he says that their stay in the enclave, make it impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse. Doesn't "en masse" include the army and the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a negative link to the sentence from the directive. That is my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you think this is incriminatory also.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "incriminatory"? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, like you --

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Like you said about the reference from Directive 7. If this refers to the civilians and saying the civilians and the army can't survive there, that's very similar to the incriminating comment that you referred to in Directive 7, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the formulation is similar. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see the term in English "survive" is similar to both of them. So given that similarity that you've acknowledged in Ognjenovic's report to his troops and the fact that he had made reference to a recent visit to Mladic to the corps command, do you think that Ognjenovic would have developed this incriminatory language himself, or is he getting that from his superior command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that there is any reference to a quotation here. I don't know how he understood the conversation. I see that this is how he transferred it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you do think he has transferred information from Mladic to this order?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He formulated that and on the basis of what, that I cannot say. He is the signatory of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you earlier relied very much on your logic. Does your logic assist you here in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does, as I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that he is the signatory and that's -- that's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every signatory of a combat document is responsible for the document and for what is expressed there, in terms of principles and in terms of powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your logic doesn't say anything about whether or not he would have done this without his superiors knowing of developing these -- this language or correcting him if it was wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is the signatory of the document and it's a public document, and I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that the formulation is bad, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first you finish -- there was one portion of your answer which was missed by the interpreters. You said, Witness: "He is the signatory of the document and it's a public document, and I don't know ..." Could you please repeat what you then said. So not extend the answer but just repeat what you then said. You do not know. And then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether anyone drew his attention to this because the document was accessible to superior commands as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question. Isn't it true that a commander of a subordinate unit has to give orders to his unit in accordance with orders received from above, from a higher level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but not orders that are contrary to the law and regulations. Such orders are not carried out and are not built into combat documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is -- would be the principle. I'm asking you more about factual proceedings. The framework is for orders of a subordinate unit is given by the upper level. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes. But it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it doesn't ... but it doesn't ... what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant that a document issuing an order cannot be a copy of all the things contained in the order of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find any document which responded to what you said was illegal approach or illegal views on what should be done or any order which was given as a consequence? Did you ever find a subordinate saying, Hey, this is illegal, I'm not going to follow your orders, or please withdraw your order? Did you find anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did, specifically the example of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade in his interim report and position regarding prisoners or, rather, prisoners of war, in the area of responsibility of his brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this document is not about prisoners of war. The portion your attention was drawn to was about making life unbearable for the population. So do you have any example of opposition or a response of the kind as I referred to against this language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And I was guided by -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've answered my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have another follow-up question. Sir, in response to a question by Judge Fluegge, you answered at page 38, line 5: "I meant that a document issuing an order cannot be a copy of all the things typed in the order of the superior command." My follow-up question is: Could a document issued by a subordinate commander expand on the order from a superior commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, expand in which sense? In terms of content, in terms of tasks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In terms of content, in terms of tasks, can it say more in its -- in the document than what was said by the superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a war, as it was waged, yes, especially in the descriptive part of the document. As for the task or objective of the activity involved, has to be expressed exactly as it was expressed in the document to the superior command. As for other elements of the document, they are derived from the document to the superior command. I mean the part that has to do with combat activities, tasks, issued to subordinate units and also securing units in terms of the combat operations involved. The first part that we are speaking of now is general, descriptive, and each and every command formulates it on the basis of its own view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And as to the objective, do you say it cannot -- can it expand the objective of the task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The task pertains to the brigade in this specific case and it cannot be expanded on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking about the objective of the task, what the task is intended to achieve. Can the subordinate expand on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objective and the task are explicitly taken over. As for this part up here, that is not in the domain of the objective and task of a specific brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, looking at the document on the screen, I read that he says: "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task." And then he tells us what that is: "The expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave." So that's what the task is supposed to achieve, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to take a look at the time of the document, when it was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You -- you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any context it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- look at the time but just answer my question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote down the time and the year and that's why I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know that but that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- not part of my question. I'm sure can you answer my question without referring to time. You can look at the time later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, if a witness is asking to see something to answer a question, I believe it is appropriate that he be allowed to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is asked a question on the basis of what is shown to him at this moment. He can answer that question and if he wants to add anything after that about time-frame and the relevance of such time-frame, he'll have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But he is being shown half of the paragraph. He is asking to see the rest of the document. I really think it's a witness's prerogative to ask to see an entirety of a document before answering a question about one small part of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think he has seen it before. But he is now invited to interpret the language of this document as it stands. Relevance of that language, time-frame, et cetera, is certainly a matter which may be raised after that, but this question can be answered without further looking to the time-frame. And, as a matter of fact, the witness has shown again and again that matters which are not asked, that he uses those not -- to evade answering a question. Therefore, he should focus now on answering that question. And perhaps Judge Moloto briefly repeats it because there has been quite an exchange of words after the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I said: "Well" - and I quote myself, this is at page 40, line 9 - "looking at the document on the screen, I read that it says: "'We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task.'" "And then he tells us what this is: 'The expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave.' "So that's what the task is supposed to achieve, isn't it?" That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the position was taken out of context and I don't think that that is its meaning. And I don't think there was a military intention to expel Muslims from Srebrenica either in that period or at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. You are now interpreting this. My question was originally: Can a subordinate expand on an order given by a superior? You said: No, not as far as objectives are concerned. But to the extent that he gives directives as to what should be done on the ground, he may. Now I'm saying here, this is an objective, objective is to expel the Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. Is that something that a subordinate could add when -- even though it was not included in the command of the superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a task and it's not an objective. In this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the final result that must come: The expulsion of the Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. Once that has been achieved, what else is there for the army to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the time of the document, that was not the objective or the task of this brigade. And it couldn't have carried out such a task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it is contained in this order, this objective. And it is at that time when -- of this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying ... Your Honour, I'm not saying that the order is a good one. It's not good. It's not precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm also not talking about its goodness or badness. I'm just talking about how orders are carried out because you explained that you can exclude some things that are coming from a superior order, and I'm asking the opposite: Can you expand on orders from the -- from superior orders? Whether the order is good or not good is not the point I am making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this first part, it is formulated in its own way. It is not simply copied. And it is not expressed verbatim as it was presented in the document to the superior command. Rather, they are operationalized and expressed in terms of the needs of one's own unit, the specific area of responsibility of the brigade, and its surrounding area. So this part of paragraph 2 does not have to be copied from the document of the superior command and doesn't have to quote that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously you are not answering my question. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, just for purposes of the record. At temporary transcript page 42, lines 10 through 12,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO SAID
utterances.text: Your interpreting the document, you're not answering the question. When in fact just prior to that, Judge Orie at transcript page 41, line 13 through 14, specifically instructed the witness to interpret the document. So I want that on the record that the witness was following Judge Orie's instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's hereby on the record whether it's -- what you said, Mr. Ivetic. It's on the record, you've said it, it's transcribed, it's there. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me also place on the record that that may be so. My question didn't ask for any interpretation. It asked for something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and that's why I did not have any problems with your questions. I just wanted it on the record that that was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General, I want to take us back where you and I had left off on this Ognjenovic document. You had agreed with me or had said that part of this document was, similar to the other one, problematic. And I refer to the section where it talks about "en masse" and "survive" there. And I want to explore that a little more because, have you had a chance to review General Zivanovic, the then-commander of the Drina Corps, his handwritten notes on meetings that occurred at the corps on July 1st, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity to see these handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, they haven't been in -- used in open court or by any -- in -- in this court yet by any witness, as far as I know. So let's take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: P5273, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, I'm just showing you a little red book, sir, with "JNA" on it. This is, we believe, to be the original copy that we -- was obtained from General Zivanovic. And it says "JNA" on it. Is that a typical officer's notebook, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it to be familiar based on the visual perception of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what we have -- because the translation is the actual handwritten document which can be difficult to read, so what we've done is we have -- if we could have in the B/C/S side only 65 ter 19193B, where we have typed up in Cyrillic precisely what we -- as best as we could, what we see in the handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think -- it should be much easier for you to look at. And if we could also hand to you the first few pages of that typed version so you can get a feel for it as we begin here with 1 July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see that the typed Cyrillic version is part of the exhibit in e-court. I only see the handwritten version. So I'm a little bit confused as to now we have a document prepared by somebody else, which is not the original, being used instead of the original that is not part of an exhibit. I could be mistaken about this but I only see two documents in e-court. One is an English translation, the other one I opened up is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there are three versions in e-court. One is the handwritten one, but let's check it, whether this is true also for this portion. Again we were talking about P...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P5273. I'll check immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we sent this to the Defence in an e-mail on Monday night to try to avoid any problem. I know you've been busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have, but whether I got it in e-mail it's still not part of the exhibit as I see it on the screen. That's my concern. I don't know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey referred to a 65 ter number and we should try to find it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see this handwritten version in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's up there. That's our typed version now. As you may remember seeing the handwritten version originally, we now have the typewritten version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the handwritten version, I found that in e-court so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with the handwritten. I'm saying that the exhibit that's been tendered, P5273, has a handwritten and has a typed version. It does not have a typed B/C/S version. Therefore, if we're using -- mixing and matches parts of two different documents, I think either something needs to be added to P5273 or -- or some more information. That's the problem I have. It might be in e-court under another number, but it doesn't address the fact that this exhibit that is being referred to now is being compared to another document without both languages of the exhibit as it's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that. Of course, the importance of it is, Mr. Ivetic, whether the typewritten version, which I remember we have used in some -- at some times, whether the typewritten version fully corresponds with the handwritten version, whether there's any dispute about the accuracy of the transcription into a typewritten version. If there's anything of the kind you are concerned about, please tell us immediately. If there's not for the time being, it should be uploaded and should be made part of the exhibit as we look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My concern is we don't have anyone in e-court -- pardon me, in the courtroom today who can do that analysis since Mr. Stojanovic can't -- actually, Mr. Stojanovic can check it. I apologise. We will have him check to see the correlation between the typed and the handwritten. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's, of course, why we sent it on Monday. And this is a convenience for the witness so he doesn't have to try to sort out the handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General, now, we're looking at General Zivanovic's handwritten notes which are dated 1 July, which we -- it's the Prosecution's position is the 1 July meeting when Mladic was at the corps that was referenced in Ognjenovic's previous document. And I can tell you, having leafed through it a bit, we can see the people noted in his notes as present at that meeting were General Mladic, Pandurevic, Andric, Krstic, Ognjenovic, Kusic, Furtula, Tolimir, Gvero.
