So those are members of -- some of those are brigade commanders of the Drina Corps and some of those were members of the Main Staff. I think we know the players at this point. So let's now explore a bit. Let's see if General Zivanovic's notes reflect anything like what we saw in Ognjenovic's document of a few days later. And remembering the issue is, is this -- the survive issue, is something that came out of the hand of an operations officer or is this something that perhaps the Main Staff has developed? So let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps it would be good if the witness has an opportunity to read through these documents during the break and that you then ask questions that he is more familiar with the text. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. You're invited to just glance through that document that has been given to you. You may follow the usher. Mr. McCloskey, as far as timing is concerned, and I'm not only addressing you but also addressing Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- we resume at quarter past 12.00. What is then to be expected. Will be able to conclude the evidence of this witness today? Mr. Ivetic is nodding yes but it takes two to tango.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I very much hope so. Let me see how much time I have taken and what else I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have approximately half an hour left. Perhaps in view of the questions by the Chamber a little bit more, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A little bit over half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will make every effort to finish that up and -- unless you really want me to continue onward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that leave you sufficient time for re-examination, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It would, Your Honours. Right now, I have 40 to 45 minutes total and I can try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's not -- I mean, we have still two breaks to go and have two hours and 15 minutes left so -- but I take it that the parties will stick to their assessments. We'll take a break and resume at -- well, now, 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to urge the witness again to try to give direct answers to the questions. That's most important. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General, let's go through these notes and see what we can make of them. We first see 1 July 1994 and then Vlasenica. Vlasenica is the location of the headquarters of the Drina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then we see General Mladic is underlined and there's several bullet points. Take a look at those. But then we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S typed because it's my understanding that this notation that General Zivanovic makes: "We are on our way to clear the enclaves." Do you see that on the note, General?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page in the English, and it should be page 3 in the typed B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see Colonel Andric there, and under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are not on the right page in B/C/S yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Should be page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Cyrillic, okay. I didn't know that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Colonel Andric, we can agree he was the brigade commander for the Sekovici Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see Mladic's name written. And then it says: "You have enough troops." Can logic tell us that General Mladic must have told Colonel Andric that he has enough troops?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense and what for? It could be a general statement or it could refer to a specific mission. We can't see from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree. But I just want -- we can agree that General Mladic said: "You have enough troops." But we don't know what he means besides that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't even know whether he said it. In fact, I don't know whether he said it or not. I have a general problem with a handbook, with a copy book as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue to go through it, despite your problems, and if there's anything I can help with, let me know. Let's now go to page 4 in the B/C/S, staying on the page we are, we see Kosoric. Wasn't there a Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric in the Drina Corps intelligence department?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see a reference to Krstic. At that time in 1994, Radislav Krstic would have been the Chief of Staff deputy commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we go to page 3 in the English, should be page 5 in the typed B/C/S, we go down and again we see Mladic's name and some bullet points. And it says here: "The enclave is not so that they survive but so that they disappear."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that does not correlate to the B/C/S that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, could we move --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Should be B/C/S page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we have is -- this is not, I think -- I'll just ... this is not the right page. This is also not the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The text was there. It's just different from -- than it is in the English. That the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go back to the page where we have above each other, I think, where Ognjenovic is supposed to start --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. And so here in the B/C/S, it says [B/C/S spoken]. Enclaves are not to survive but to disappear. So the additional, "that they," is not in the B/C/S that is in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is your -- whether that's an accurate translation or not, that is how -- that is for CLSS to decide. But we are now, I think, on the right page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And this was a recently revised CLSS translation and I would -- if we have these issues, we can discuss it outside the presence of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any matter remaining, then I take it that it will be either agreed by the parties upon or it will be sent to CLSS to specifically verify this portion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The term "survive" is similar to the terms used in Directive 7 and in Ognjenovic's document we saw from 1994, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term itself, yes, but the meaning is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, well, we see the meaning as: "The enclave is not so they survive but so that they disappear," and I think we'll leave it at that. As we go down farther, we can see under Mladic - this is -- should be B/C/S the next page, page 6 on my note - "reduce the enclave." All right. Now let's -- we've seen Zivanovic's note. Let's take a look at Zivanovic's other notebook for 1995 which we also got from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we do so. The Chamber would like to have that one sentence over the next break be reviewed by CLSS if that's possible - it's just one sentence - to see whether there's really some different meaning. Mr. Ivetic raised the matter. Whether it's just language or whether it's more, we do not know, and we'd like to have that one sentence be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We were concerned and did that a few days ago, and my only request would be if we try to get the same -- not that there's many people left at CLSS, but if we have the same group, then we will be on better grounds. Because you know languages better than I are not perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But was it specifically focusing on that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that sentence was confirmed as having received an accurate translation by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is CLSS focusing on this. We asked them to, and this is what they gave us and that was provided the Defence. This has all been done days before, though I know Mr. Ivetic has been busy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under those circumstances, Mr. Ivetic, I think it would not have been appropriate to say what it says in English and whether it's right or wrong. If you are aware of this verification --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then you should have raised -- you were not informed about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I, as I stand here, am not aware of that. And I'm reading what is the official text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and this new document that was given to me on Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- so when it could have been confirmed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand now and if there's any doubt about that, of course, that should be sorted out, but that specifically this line has been verified by CLSS very recently, focusing especially on this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we leave it to that. And if there's any doubt, then the party which wishes to raise that has an opportunity to do so. But, meanwhile, we'll continue. And I withdraw the Chamber's request of having this one line being confirmed during the next break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so it's clear, the typed Cyrillic is not a translation of anything. It's -- it's a transcript of the handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So we're back to P05274, page 25 in the English, and if we, doing the same thing we did before, go to 65 ter 19192B, page 1. The P number was P5274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is not the corresponding page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The 65 ter was 19192B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is a 54 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm sorry, I must have the wrong number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we have now is 54 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's just go to the handwritten, then, that goes along with the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh. Okay. Thank you. Don't know where I went wrong there, but thank you for getting it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General, we can see that -- well, it's off my page, but if we can make the English bigger, there should be a date - there we go - of 8 March 1995. We'll make yours bigger as well, so hopefully you can see that. It should be there. Yeah. And as we'll recall that was the date on the doc -- on Directive 7 that Karadzic signed, and we see it says "GS - KM." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it conveniently lists who is present. We see Mladic and General Tomic. General Tomic was the finance and planning chief, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Colonel Skrbic was in personnel?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've told us about Colonel Beara, and we know about Colonel Ognjenovic. And we have discussions referred here. So let's go to the next page in English, should be the next page in the Serbian as well. And we see that someone is -- says that they are ashamed because they're not a colonel. And that continues. We get into a bit about UNPROFOR, enemy aircraft towards Srebrenica, bring down. That's -- Mladic's name is written next to that. Then it says: In Srebrenica - details control. Then Mladic's name is written. So let's go to the next page, and what we see here is a note that Zivanovic has written down: "Make life impossible." That is similar to what we see in the language that you've spoken of in Directive 7 and in Ognjenovic's report of 1994, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago, I reviewed now and I reviewed during the break these words, and I cannot say based on words in a copy book what somebody had in mind and what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, that wasn't the question. Would you agree with me that it's similar to the -- what was -- you called it the incriminatory language of Directive 7 and the language in Ognjenovic's order of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it relates to. I don't see it from here. Of course, it's incriminating. "Make life impossible." But what does this simple sentence relate to? To whom? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not there yet. We're just looking at whether this is a corresponding textual element to the documents we have been shown before. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we'll leave those final questions to the Chamber on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But with one question. You have said that it's an operations officer of some sort, we don't really know if it's an officer or an enlisted man, that made this mistake and it got overlooked by several people. Now that you have seen this same similar topic of survival and making life impossible discussed at the highest levels of the VRS, does your logic tell you that perhaps you're wrong about that this is -- this is something that's coming only from an operations guy that made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My logic tells me that this copy book displayed in this way, expressed in this way, does not reflect the essence. When I analyse a combat document, I understand it. A copy book of an individual doesn't mean anything to me, nor can I conclude what it's about based on one or two words in a paragraph. I have no idea what the writer meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned when we were talking about the self-organised paramilitaries and groups of avengers working with or being -- co-ordinating with security officers, you as an example gave the Skorpion unit. So I take it you're aware of the -- the film where ten members of the Skorpion unit can be seen together with six Muslim men and boys and then at some point we see those men and boys, like you say, shot in the back?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take to you a document, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness answered in the affirmative. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was half nodding, half -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 01931.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As that's coming up there, General, were you aware -- when you described Sarajevo you said one of the sections, I think, was the Trnovo area and so I think you're familiar with some of the combat and situations that were going on in the Trnovo area in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents, yes. From several documents. I mean primarily the monographs of the commander and the Chief of Staff of the 1st Corps and the combat documents of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see from those documents that the Drina Corps had to send units to assist the Serb forces on the -- at the Trnovo front?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you -- did you note that one of those forces was a temporarily created brigade called the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a unit of temporary composition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this document which is on this general topic, and I think we can all see from looking at the Serbian version that is it typed signed Ratko Mladic, SR. It's dated 19 July. And I really just want to touch base briefly on what this document's about. We see in the second paragraph it's a -- it's a reference to the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade command for troop rotation in Trnovo. And if we look at General Mladic's order, point 1, he explains that due to the Drina Corps units' activities regarding the liberation of Zepa, searching the terrain, and blocking and destroying the remnants of Muslim groups from Srebrenica in the greater area of Cerska, Kamenica, and Pobudje, the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade remains at its present combat positions in the greater Trnovo until further notice. So the -- by the 19th of July, the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade is still stuck in Trnovo; correct? On Mladic's orders? Is that correct? I'm sorry, if you answered, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Okay. Now I want to show you, and I'm not going into great detail, I don't think it's necessary, but a map we picked up from the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could start off with 65 ter 33401. And if I could hand a bigger version, I think it will be helpful for the General to take a look at. We've provided these maps in big form to the Defence a few days ago. If he could just take a look at it to familiarize himself with it. And for the English readers, could we blow up the top so we can get an idea of what that says. The top left. Okay. And we see that it's the work map of the chief of intelligence and security of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade, which is printed out over the top of Sarajevo. Now can we go back and look at the blue marks on this map, kind of blow up the blue part, and with the English translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, what I wanted to ask you about is, very briefly, what is this? We see blue, we see red. Is this a sketch of the Muslim positions and -- in blue and the Serb positions in red?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslim or Bosniak forces are marked blue and the red are Serbian. But a good part of the Muslim forces are in the area that was controlled by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just in the very south of this map, our English tell us that one of the initials of the Serb forces is the 1/4, which has been translated as the 1st Battalion of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade. Is that your understanding of that -- that -- those initials down in the bottom south of the -- of this map, for the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I offer this into evidence, this -- this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and also could I offer 01931 into evidence too. That was the Mladic map -- excuse me, the Mladic order regarding the rotation of troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7712, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7712 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you repeat the 65 ter number of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 01931. Now can we go to 65 ter number 33469.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, we can see, if we look at the Serbian sides, that this is from the commander, Major-General Radislav Krstic. And I really just want to get from you, we see what -- what this is. It's talking about the transportation of men from the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade and it issues an order in that effect. And it gives the route by which the men from these units are to go to get to Trnovo. And we can see that it's direction Bratunac, Milici, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, Sokolac, Pale, Dobre Vode, Trnovo. That's in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'd like to offer that into evidence and get a map that up will help us with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think there have to be questions asked of the witness if they're going to offer a document through a witness. I don't see that one has as to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's absolutely right. I asked -- I forgot to say: Am I correct in the reading of that and my interpretation of it. It's a bad way to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation. I just heard the document itself. What you said is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it is basically Krstic giving the directions of where the unit providing the reinforcements to Trnovo is to go; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the superior officer that was his obligation as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If could I offer that in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 33469 will be Exhibit P7713.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7713 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you have a good working knowledge of the important locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you -- you have a working knowledge of roughly where the front lines were, very roughly, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's true when you -- people had to travel during the war time they had to, of course -- both sides had to take into account where those fronts lines were, so direct route to places may not have been as direct as they would have been in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. One had to go around many roads, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 33523.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if this will help, you could take a look at it. It's another map that we provided to the Defence. And it's actually a composite of two maps that are already in evidence, so we've been able to put the -- roughly where the front lines were from those other two maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just in looking at the maps, all we've really done here is, aside from helping remind you of roughly where the front lines were, we've noted the areas that we found on the map, the various cities, and plotted them out towards Trnovo and then onto the village of Turovi. Does that roughly accord to the locations that you -- that you recall and would those be the right locations for the various towns and villages that we've noted here?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this copy is not exactly legible. It's only the names that can be seen, and the lines, sort of. Now, to what extent this is right, to what extent it corresponds, I really cannot say. It cannot be seen very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not meant -- it's meant to show the towns in relation to the front lines and their general position. Does it roughly accord with your recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7714, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7714 is admitted. Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Ivetic you gave an estimate of 40 minutes. Is that still - I have to ask you - a valid estimate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40, 45. Then, Mr. McCloskey, you've used approximately your time by now. There were five minutes left. Could you try to conclude in ten minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will try to get through this in -- in five minutes. And there was one more document that was in response to the issue that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you use your time to do what you can do in those ten minutes, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We need P3096.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll soon be seeing, General, a document from Dragomir Milosevic, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, dated 23 July 1995, and it's a regular combat report to the Main Staff of the VRS. And I just want to note a couple of the things that -- here and ask you to help me. Under "the enemy" it says: "The enemy forces attacked our units at Trnovo line during the day. That is at 1145 hours. The most violent attack was launched at the Runjevic feature, the point of convergence between the Ministry of Interior, MUP (Skorpions) and the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade." And then it describes the weapons used. And then under "our forces," it says: "The MUP units (Skorpions) and the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade successfully repelled the enemy attack and inflicted heavy losses on the enemy." And then it describes some more and it actually describes that in paragraph 3, that there were -- some Skorpions were wounded as well as the other forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we could go to -- it's a cutout from the big map that you saw that was the combat map from the Drina Brigade. This should be 65 ter 33505. Now, if we could blow that up a little bit, centring on the centre of the map right now. Okay. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the centre, we see the Runjevica feature where the -- were the 1st Battalion of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade is noted in handwriting. Would that be the feature referred to in Milosevic's report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in that report, it says that the attack was launched at the convergence between the Skorpion and the Drina units. Can you tell us, militarily, would those two units be side by side normally in a defence line or would they be all mixed up together?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war time, there were different situations and the speed was there to react to attacks by the other side. As for this area, specifically in this period, according to Muslim sources and according to Serb sources, was a period of intensive offensive activities when the Serb forces did not have enough units. So both --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General -- I'm sorry, General. I -- it was a simple question. Are -- the Skorpions unit are adjacent to the Drina unit, right? They're not all mixed up as they are on that defence line?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what was said here, next to, adjacent to. And in principle, forces do not mix. But you asked me in principle whether such cases were possible and that's how I answered. But what I found out was adjacent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put an SK on that Runjevic feature so that we can note that that's where they -- that's where that attack came at them, the Skorpions and the Drina outfit? I know we don't know at this point know exactly where they were, but just put it anywhere on the Runjevic feature since we do know that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assume where this smaller unit was. This is a small unit in terms of its number of personnel. And on a map like this, it can be 4 millimetres on the slopes of Runjevica to the south-west of Runjevica. So I cannot put something there that I cannot see in the text itself. I cannot see the exact position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, and that's a fair point. I don't want the exact position, and I just -- if you can just mark generally SK so that we can reflect that you agree that this is the feature where the two units fought the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was interpreted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Mr. McCloskey, we see where it says "1/4,DLPB," we see Runjevica close to the elevation 992 there. If that is the area you are referring to. If that's the area I think the witness said was what was referred to, then we don't need it any further if the map is there. Even without the marking we would know what part is dealt with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here that this -- the red line to the far left, as we look at it, basically goes in a roughly north/south direction. And from this document, we don't know whether the Skorpions are on the north of the Drina units or the south, do be?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot see it on the basis of the document either. That's what I said that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you know or do you not know? If you don't know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your last two or three minutes have started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to P07588. Oh, sorry, could we put this in evidence first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's good that you asked already for the next document so that it will be there. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33505 will be Exhibit P7715, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document from the police force staff to the office of the minister, the Pale police force staff. So this is a MUP document. And this describes the location of the MUP forces as they're laid out, and I briefly would direct you to that. And I specifically note that it says: "The defence line as far as above Turovi village is held by a PJP company from Doboj and a police company from Jahorina. And on the right of the company from Doboj facing" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. McCloskey please indicate where he is reading from in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the middle. "And on the right of the company from Doboj facing Runjevica, the defence line is held by the Skorpije MUP of Serbia." Now, can we go back to the last map we had up on the board, 7715. P7715.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, it's the position of the Prosecutor that if you go to the Turovi village, which we see in this map in the bottom near the right, and we go up as described, that show -- that would indicate that the Skorpions are to the south of the 1st Battalion of the 4th Light Infantry Brigade. Just take a look at the document a little bit, if you'd like. And I can hand that to you so you can look at the map and the document at the same time. And if you agree or disagree or you don't know, either -- any of those are, of course, appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that based on the information in that report, that that would show that the Skorpion unit are to the south of the Drina Light Infantry Brigade? Because while it doesn't mention the light infantry brigade in that document, it does note the units as going up towards the north, to the Runjevic feature. But, again, I -- I leave that up to you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago, when it was being read out, it said to the right of the Drina Light Infantry Brigade. It's probably a reference to this 1st Battalion. And now on this basis it is concluded, according to the text, that it is to the left. So it can be to the left, south-west of the 1st Battalion of the 4th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the time is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have one more map that would tie this into the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The time is over. That's -- because otherwise you've spent more time than you asked for. The Defence still needs another 45 minutes, 40 to 45 minutes. They'll get 40. We leave it to that. But let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm overruled, Mr. McCloskey. But then we should prepare for at least some -- a little bit of additional time beyond quarter past 2.00. I hope that that will be available. Otherwise we would have to have a session tomorrow for 15 or 20 minutes, which is not something I think the parties were seeking, neither is the Chamber. One map. Try to deal with it as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 33517.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned you looked at the materials, or you know about the Skorpion murders. And this map will be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we -- I think that needs to be gone back a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, my eyes are not seeing what I'm having to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What you're seeing is, of course, the Runjevic feature and what we have -- the Prosecution has marked on this map in yellow boxes the co-ordinate of where the -- a body was picked up, and in the area of the mass executions of these people, the house location is where a house that is seen on the video is -- is -- was noted in the -- in the film and the arrival site is along the road where the people were in a -- in a truck. Now, we can see that this execution area is very close to the front line where the Skorpions were wounded on the 23rd of July. My -- my last question on this topic is: To pull ten people off a very important defence line, would that not have to be authorised by the superiors in -- in charge of that defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Misstates the evidence. The witness on this topic did not say they were pulled from the front line. He said the opposite. It is RM280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know whether -- were you quoting the evidence, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey was putting a question to the witness, not necessarily quoting what the evidence was at the time. And therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Foundation is a -- I think that Mr. McCloskey may put this question to the witness. If there's any foundational issue, you can revisit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please again put the question to the witness, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, if ten members of a unit were on that front line, would they not have to have the authorisation of their superiors to be pulled off it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this is a MUP unit and we can see on the basis of all of this, they had their own area of responsibility. And I said already at the outset I saw that footage several times. I think that it was made by murderers, professional murderers, with the intention of selling that footage later on and in order to discredit the struggle of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're going far beyond the question that was put to you and thus you're abusing the time available to Mr. McCloskey. The answer was no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 33517 will be Exhibit P7716, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that ends my presentation. I did -- there was one question related to questions asked by Judge Moloto that I have one document about. I don't want to keep us here. I don't want to us be in court tomorrow, but I do have that. That would maybe take five minutes, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then first check at all whether we could have a extended session. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes is, as I'm told, possible. Which means that if you would stop in four minutes from now, we would have a break and resume at a quarter to 2.00 and Mr. Ivetic would have 45 minutes. And I see Mr. Mladic is nodding that he agrees. P7716 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 2318 up on the board. And let's get the Serbian up. And could we blow up the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we see that this is noted to be a transcript of an audio-taped recording of a conversation between Colonel General Ratko Mladic and Dusan Kozic, prime minister of the RS, 23 October 1995 at 1640 hours. And then we see handwritten: "Tosa, they took it all down well, I'm only not sure whom he mentioned in addition to Djukanovic." And then we see this initial. Do you recognise General Mladic's initial?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen his initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's the Prosecution's position the initials next to that are the initials of Zdravko Tolimir. Have you ever seen Zdravko Tolimir's initials?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only signatures on combat documents. I've never seen his initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know that Tosa was Tolimir's nickname that Mladic used to call him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was a young officer at that time, a captain. I was not familiar with that level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 12 of this transcripted conversation in English, and B/C/S page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they're talking about some sort of a job to do, and Kozic concludes in the middle of the page: "So it means Beara." And Mladic responds: "No, if only it was Beara. Beara wouldn't do anything to bypass the system, anything to bypass my orders. Beara is in the cross-hairs, poor man." And then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think the question misstates the document. They're not talking about some kind of job. They're talking about the fallen pilots. So if you're going to present a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't heard a question yet if I -- apart from that, Mr. Ivetic, you're invited not already to stand when you're still waiting for making an objection, but rather jump up if you make an objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that contradicts your view that you expressed earlier, that Colonel Beara would be acting on his own without Mladic's knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object to the question. Misstates the prior evidence which was in relation to events in Srebrenica. This has not been tied to Srebrenica, at least not in the question, not in the text I've read, and I've read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree. It's not about Srebrenica. It's about the relationship between Beara and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can answer the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Beara was a renegade in that sense and that he wasn't complying with orders. But what he was doing there and that communication that I saw in the documents indicates that he was doing that on his own as part of his job in co-operation with the subordinate security organs and that he didn't need any approval for that. No special approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this particular document suggests that Beara would be very loyal to General Mladic and follow his orders, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything about loyalty. I see that he is subordinate, not in the first line of subordination but the second line of subordination in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think we now really came to the point. The witness has answered this question. We are at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't give me a chance to close, Your Honour. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given the closure, I have a follow-up question which I -- which I had earlier but let pass, but now this topic is being come backed to. When we talked about Beara earlier in the day and you said that he did what he did without Mladic's consent, I wanted -- you said Mladic didn't have the jurisdiction to discipline but he could initiate proceedings. Are you aware of any proceedings that he initiated in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he ever found out or whether he initiated proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question. The question is: Are you aware of proceedings that he initiated whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, could I offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, and could the witness already be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 02318 will be Exhibit P7717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7717 is admitted into evidence. We take a break. We'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00. What is not yet on the record is that I said that I saw Mr. Mladic confirming and nodding that he had -- did not object to such an extended session. We take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed. Witness, could I you urge you again to try to answer the questions as directly as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at P1505 which was shown to you today. This was shown to you today in relation to questions relating about orders, relating about tasks, et cetera. Looking at the heading on this document, [Interpretation] "Information for brigade members, submitted to," [In English] is this document a command document, that is to say, an order of any type?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not an order. It's just information as envisaged by documents made, prepared in unit commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the next questions we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, at the very beginning of your cross-examination by the Prosecution, you were asked about two documents that had the word "ciscenje," and these were P7664 and P7665. Although Mr. Weber promised that he would get to the definition of that word with you at transcript page 41581, lines 13 through 16, in fact, he did not. Militarily speaking, can you give us a definition of the term "ciscenje teren," or "cleansing of the terrain" in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was just making sure it was working. I believe that the documents didn't refer -- Mr. Ivetic is now asking for a definition of something more than what, I guess, I was referring to. I referred to ciscenje, he's adding the -- now a factor that did not derive from I believe I was originally drawing the attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- well, the main issue is not and I even wondered whether there was any need to tell that did not ask, et cetera. Mr. Ivetic is now asking a question, and we'll later find out whether it's about the same subject as you dealt with or whether there's any difference. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, can you answer. What is the definition of "ciscenje teren"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terminology, clearing or cleansing is a concept that means searching the terrain for armed enemy formations in the area of responsibility, in the area of action, or the area of employment of forces. So within one's own disposition or in the area of use of forces, and it pertains to armed units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In a military sense, is there any difference between ciscenje and ciscenje teren?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ciscenje is a general term, whereas clearing the terrain means, in fact, pertains to armed elements armed units, terrorists, sabotage groups, et cetera. That's what cleansing or clearing the terrain would mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you were asked about P7667.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to call that document up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see here the document is from the SDB, state security sector. It mentions SDB and MUP. Would either the SDB or MUP, under normal conditions, be services that fall under the command structure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the appearance and format of this report, does it resemble -- does it have the elements that would be expected of a report sent to a military commander of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any military elements. I see information or intelligence that falls within their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Early in the cross-examination you were questioned at length about portions of your expert report that rely upon Professor Radinovic. In relation to those paragraphs where you adopted text or conclusions shared by Professor Radinovic, what steps did you take to verify the information at issue before using the same?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the database of the original documents given me for review that I indicated at the beginning of my testimony. That means the database of the forces of the VRS and partly documents of the BiH army and some of the HVO, but there were much less of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did Professor Radinovic know that you were preparing an expert report for this case?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, we contact -- we were in contact a lot while he was making his expert report for Karadzic and while I was making mine for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did Professor Radinovic ever voice any objection to your use of materials from his own expert reports?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. He gave me himself his material and even his documents and some monographs and books, and sometimes we discussed the findings that he arrived at and that I arrived myself at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now call up P7086.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for it, this was a document you were asked about at transcript page 41578. And we'll see it's from the command of the Birac Brigade and signed by Major Svetozar Andric. Andric testified at this trial, at transcript page 34773 to 34775, about this, and I'd like to quote two parts of his testimony about this order to you. The first part is as follows: "This order pertained to all, not only Muslims. Serbs were also moving out because this was a combat area. So at the same time Serbs left, went to Zvornik and Srbinje. In order to protect the people there I ordered that women and children be allowed to go to Kalesija and Gracanica because of combat operations. Then also because of revenge. "People, refugees were coming in from Gracanica, Kalesija, Tuzla, and we had to prevent any kind of revenge that could be taken by them, and that is why I have to say that it is precisely this order of mine that saved thousands of people. Had we left these people in the combat area, I believe that many would not be alive today. So it is precisely this order that contributed. "And later on, we will see that the same persons were exchanged and that to this day they live together with their families." And the second part of the testimony in relation to this document is as follows: "I don't know whether -- well, from the combat zone, both Muslims and Serbs were moved out because that was basically a front line. We did not have any depth in our front, Mr. President. We did not have a depth of the front. We just had the front line. So how could you control what was happening in depth? Just one example: A brigade defends 10 to 15 kilometres principle, whereas the zone of my brigade is 150 kilometres. 150 kilometres. Along one line you have 100 kilometres in depth. You cannot prevent revenge. You cannot --" And that's where the testimony ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see counsel on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, I do not believe that this fully accurately conveys the testimony related to the document in particular. I would just note that a portion on page 34775 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, if you think it's taken out of context, you have an opportunity to address that later --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But just for the record, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're inviting Mr. Ivetic to read that to the witness. I have it in front of me so I know exactly what -- that it was a literal quote but it was not all of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you understand what Andric is talking about in relation to, first, removing people from combat zone, and then, second, this concept depth of the front? From a military perspective what are those two concepts?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I see it, this testimony represents the actual conditions on the ground. It's one month into the beginning of the civil war and the commander was not able to -- with those forces that had not yet been established as a proper army was not able to control even the front line, let alone behind the lines, and deal with various groups in villages and populated areas. This approach to the departure of the population under the control of the armed forces was, indeed, an act of salvation, an act of rescue, in the whole combat area and in the area of Podrinje generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now move to P3822 which was also shown to you by the Prosecution. That's at transcript page 41580 and onwards. And once we pull up that document, I'd like to look at the -- exactly the part that the Prosecution highlighted which was section 1b. General, if you look at the text contained in this combat report, in section 1b, and keep in mind my question which is: From a military perspective, if a professionally trained military officer were to receive such a report, would it, in your opinion, put him on notice of any potential wrong-doing on the part of subordinate soldiers? So please read 1b to yourself and then let us know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the term is used here in the meaning of the basic military concept, and it pertains to armed groups and units in that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now let's keep in mind this document is dated 22 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at an earlier document, P718, which is from the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade dated 22 August 1992. And if we can go to the second page in both, I'm looking for the -- yes, the very last part of this document that says: "Within this territory in the villages of Micivode, Raktitnica, Kramer Selo, and Novoseoci, there is a certain number of extremists who are peaceful for now. They are not causing problems to the Serbian population but we are keeping them under control."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If there are extremists in an area, the same area that was the subject of the last document we looked at, do you consider the military actions that were reported in the previous document to be appropriate to handle extremists?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at D130, and this will be dated 27 July 1992 from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and I would ask that we focus on the second paragraph. It's the second paragraph, part 1. And the translation is a little bit different than the one I have so I'll read from the screen. And it says: "Muslim population surrendered their weapons and lethal assets to representatives of the 2nd Romanija Brigade in the village of Novoseoci, 5 to 6 kilometres south of Sokolac, Glasinacko Polje. The surrender was done as agreed, and it is believed not all of the weapons have been surrendered." In your opinion, would the existence of armed extremists in this area justify the actions of the army that were reported in the report -- combat report that we just looked at from September 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's simply a necessary measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D5358, paragraph 4.220 of the same, which should be ... should be on page 177 of the B/C/S, 179 and 180 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is in relation to the couple that was killed on the Vrbanja bridge. And during cross-examination you were asked about this text being identical only to Wikipedia and not other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask that 65 ter 1D6179 be called up. It is a Serbian-language newspaper, "Kurir," from its web site, dated 18 May 2013. And we have a draft translation that we have prepared and I have a hard copy for the witness, with the help of the usher. And we see here that this publicly available document does talk about the burial in Lukavica, does talk about the burial at the request of Admira's parents in Sarajevo cemetery afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd ask to you look at the Serbian original of this document, compare it to paragraph 4.220 of your report, and tell us if this is perhaps one of the other sources that you identified at transcript page 41534, line 24 and onwards, during the cross-examination, in addition to the Wikipedia page?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the sources. There were quite a few other papers that provided information about the event. I'm sorry that the essence of the crime was not referred to then, the crime perpetrated by the special forces of the Muslims. Because one can see how monstrous this was, the planning of the crime and its purpose, that was attained within the media war concerning this so-called siege of Sarajevo and the terrorisation of the civilian position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness with respect to this. You said you used this also in preparing your report. Why is it not footnoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said then as well that with regard to one and the same thing, I would have six or seven sources and then I would refer to one of the sources, simply so that one of these sources could be found there. That's it. That's the main reason. If I were to footnote all the sources that I used, then I would have done that. It's just that I wrote the way any monograph is written. That was my style of writing. So that was one of the sources, so there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would tender this to be marked for identification since the English translation is not an official one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so, I just want to say that line of examination was leading, Mr. Ivetic. You could have asked the witness quite simply what other sources did you consult and could lead that, rather than show him this and then ask him: Is this one of the sources that you could have -- that you may have looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He was already asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the transcript section that I referenced, he was already asked and he said he looked at a variety of other sources including other newspaper articles. The Prosecution said this text could only be found in Wikipedia. We found that it's found in other articles as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all know that. We all know that, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You could have asked him, you, yourself, what other sources did he consult rather than show him that. That's what's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just for my ... yes. Please proceed. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I asked for it to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection. I believe this just goes to the -- further the issue of transparency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D1365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked at transcript page 41644 about your criticism of civilians in Sarajevo that did not leave the front lines. And that was in relation to paragraph 4.148 of your report, which is at page 153 English and Serbian page 150. I'd like to look at a document with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D6180. It is from the International Committee of the Red Cross from their official web site. Again, it's 1D6180. And I'd first like to turn to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the part under ICRC at the top says: "To fulfil its task of disseminating IHL, the ICRC has delegates around the world teaching armed and security forces that: 'A military objective remains a military objective even if civilian persons are in it. The civilian persons within such an objective or its immediate surrounds share the danger to which it is exposed.'" Is what is written here consistent with your understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just -- continuing the concern expressed by Judge Moloto, I'm a little concerned about just the non-open-ended nature of the information. If there was a question that was posed, that then there's a further explanation of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with his understanding of the law. We're asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you can also lead a witness in his understanding of the law, so these two are unrelated. The objection is leading. Your answer is: I can lead if it is about the understanding of the law. And I don't think that that's -- that's an exception to the -- but -- but let's just -- Mr. Weber has expressed his concern. That's it. You have answered to that. Let's ask the witness to answer -- let's ask the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in this sense, civilian facilities -- civilian buildings taken by military forces are unfortunately targets. And may I present the following position here? Now, I don't know whether this was mistakenly stated to the information. I did not say that civilians, that it was their fault because they didn't take care of themselves. On the contrary. I insisted that military forces and the authorities should have removed civilians on the Serb side and on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We do object to it. I mean, in the context that it is being offered, it is not clear even in relation to the witness's answer, the relevance is unclear at this time, and we do not have the full context of the document, I believe, even before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We do have the full document in its entirety. It's, I believe, ten pages or nine pages. It's the law. It's to help Your Honours know the law. It is entered from the bar table. As the Prosecution did with at least 2.000 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, strong language doesn't make strong arguments because you always opposed against this calling from the bar table. But if you would like to have it admitted because it's relevant in the context of the testimony of the witness, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would -- could you please upload the relevant page of this 1987 document apparently where it appears, whereas you know that we have extensive 2005 documentation of the ICRC. But if you could upload the relevant page so as to -- so that the Chamber knows the law better, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this entire document of nine pages is a summation of the law published by the ICRC. These are their citations from their official web site. They have the law for Canada, Angola, Belgium, France, United States, it's all in this document with citations. I'm asking for this document to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want the whole of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's nine pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only the ICRC part but also Oppenheim, America's Watch, Africa Watch, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we need further submissions of the parties and also an opportunity to further read the matter because these are complex matters. Civilians inside a military objective is a rather complex legal issue, as you may be aware of, and touches upon other matters as well. I would -- under those circumstances, I would postpone a decision on admission and invite the parties to make further submissions on this way of teaching the law to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. And I don't think -- we don't have a translation in B/C/S yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another reason to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up P431 and look at page 35 in the Serbian, page 43 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This was shown to you by Mr. Weber at transcript page 41634 and it is General Mladic's speech at the 16th National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I assume that we'll go to the pages that I hopefully cited correctly. My transcript is non-responsive. Again, it's page 35 in the B/C/S and page 43 in the English. And we don't need to read the whole thing but it's there so people can see that I'm not changing the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the comments of not taking prisoners, and if you read the entire selection, we see that the talk is about mercenaries. And there are no conventions in international law binding to us as far as he, a mercenary, is concerned. What is your knowledge of the status of mercenaries under the Geneva Conventions, especially Article 47 of the Additional Protocols? Do they share protections offered to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That goes for national legislation as well. That's the way it was in the former SFRY. And that is what the regulations of the newly created states say too. Mercenaries are a category of people who do not enjoy all the protection that imprisoned military personnel do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, again, you are referring to Article 47 of the Additional Protocols, that's in the plural. Does that mean that you meant --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I meant protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then which Additional Protocol did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding it is protocol. That's what I have written down, and let me just double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware that there are more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1977? Which one were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Additional Protocols. The witness has answered. I can ask the witness if he knows which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have the text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want you if you refer in a question to Additional Protocols, if there are more of them, and unless you say they all have like common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, they all have a common Article 47 in those protocols, if you don't say that, then I think you are putting a question which might confuse the witness. Because if there is no such Article 47 common to the Additional Protocols we have a problem in understanding the question. At least I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: AP, Roman I, Article 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are referring to first Additional Protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could you -- specifically the question was directly in relation to Article 47 of the first protocol. Are you aware of the content of it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not directly. That article. I spoke in principle about the difference in status between a mercenary and a military prisoner of war. I am not that familiar with legal norms, so I cannot know exactly what is defined in each and every article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you read the relevant portion to the witness. If you insist. And otherwise we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was satisfied with his answer especially with the national legislation. I have just one other question and it's to ask him to look at that map which to his left. A copy has been given to the Prosecution last week. We've also seen it this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to see if we can identify if that is one of the maps that was listed as an attachment to his report since this is the one that was -- could not be scanned and had to be sent to me in hard copy and I honestly don't know if this is one of those or not.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have no further questions on that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm done. I apologise. We've gone a little bit over the time that was foreseen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at you, Mr. Weber, Mr. McCloskey, we really have -- we have an extended session but we should finish in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Then let me see whether we have any further questions. Let me check one tiny little thing. I have no further questions for you either. Mr. Kovac, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having waited very patiently a few occasions because your testimony was interrupted several times. We highly appreciated that -- we highly appreciate that you made yourself available in this way. You've answered the questions that were put to you by the parties, by the Bench. We wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness is actually excused, we had that handwritten document of the comparison of the paragraphs originally that the witness provided to the Chamber and we do have a present in court. We have no objection to having it being returned to the witness before he leaves. We have scanned it in. I just wanted to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If -- if you would -- The original will you returned to you -- yes. The original is now returned to you. A copy has been made but that you have at least also your own copy, which is the original copy of the notes you made. Thank you again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and the week, but not after having thanked all those assisting us deeply for, again, their flexibility. It's now for a second day. Also, Mr. Mladic for making it possible for -- to have no session tomorrow, which I think would suit the parties very well. Thanks to all. We adjourn until Monday, the 30th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of November, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 25
